mappings.note: Ratio of volumes of two separate cones of equal radius. Comparison of one basic formula applied twice, not a combination (C-7.2-LO-3) and not a recast.
Cone and cylinder compared through their curved-surface formulas; they are never joined, so C-7.2-LO-2 does not apply.
Lateral surface ratio of two separate cylinders of equal height - single-solid formula used twice.
Volume ratio of two separate cylinders of equal height. Nothing is combined or converted.
Sphere melted and drawn into wire: volume conserved across a change of shape, which is exactly C-7.3-LO-3.
Qualitative - how a ball seats on a tapering cone, so more than half stays outside. No area or volume is evaluated, only how the two components meet, which is the recognition step C-7.1-LO-4 names.

Two hemispheres joined: the point is the two flat faces are no longer exposed, so only curved parts are added. Choosing which component areas count, not computing a composite total, so C-7.1-LO-4 over C-7.2-LO-2.
Cuboid moulded into a sphere - one solid form becomes another, volume equated.
Cylinder melted into twelve equal spheres; count follows from equating volumes across the shape change.

Answer is an expression, pi r(r + 2h + l), assembled by deciding which faces of a cone-on-cylinder show and which is hidden at the join. That selection is C-7.1-LO-4; no number is produced, so C-7.2-LO-2 would overstate it. (Stem references a figure that is not carried with it.)
Cuboid melted and recast into cones, count wanted. Recast-with-count, so C-7.3-LO-3 not C-7.2-LO-3.
One cylinder: divide volume by curved surface area to recover r, then h. Single solid throughout, so no combination outcome fits.
A rolled sheet becomes the curved surface of one cylinder; the 22 cm side is the base circumference. Single-solid surface relation, not a recast of a solid body.
Cylinder : cone : hemisphere volumes at equal base and height, giving 3 : 1 : 2. Three basic solids compared side by side, never joined, so not C-7.2-LO-3.
Direct volume of one cylinder. The plainest single-solid item in the chapter; no LO in this frame covers one solid.

Total surface area of a solid hemisphere, 3 pi r^2, as standard basic-solid knowledge. C-7.1-LO-4 is reserved for items where deciding which faces survive a cut or a join IS the question; here the hemisphere is given as the solid.
A sphere is halved and the whole surface of BOTH parts is wanted: 6 pi r^2, not 4 pi r^2, because the cut creates two new discs. Recognising the newly exposed faces is the discriminating step.
Volume ratio of two cylinders from ratios of r and h. Two separate solids compared, no combination.
Halving one cylinder's radius and comparing volumes - single-solid scaling, r^2 dependence.
Sphere volume ratio converted to surface-area ratio. Two separate spheres; comparison only.
Volume of the largest cone cut from a cube: read r and h off the cube, then one cone formula. The remaining solid is not asked for, so no subtraction and no C-7.2-LO-3.
Hemispherical bowl: rim circumference gives r, then capacity (2/3)pi r^3. One solid, given as a hemisphere rather than cut in the question.
Sets a single hemisphere's volume numerically equal to its surface area to recover the diameter. One solid, both formulas used on it.
Three balls melted into one - volume conserved across the merge. Melting makes this C-7.3-LO-3, not a combination of solids standing together.
Sphere recast as a cone of given height; base radius follows from equating volumes.
